reason: Examples describe the sac or the crest on the lip, not the lip itself. A rule would need to attach the quality to the sac or crest. A globose lip as a whole is rare.
Caudicles (orchid pollinium stalks) can be linear.
Parallelodromous is a venation pattern. The examples say the lobes lie parallel to each other, which is orientation, so this is a wrong reading.
A paraphysis can have an obconical head. The examples name the head, so the quality is really on a sub-part, but it is acceptable.
A costa (moss midrib) can be keeled in cross-section.
Presence of an arillode is a normal character. The examples are correct.
An androgynophore can be tomentose.
A floral corona, or its lobes, can be stellate. 'Spreading' in the examples is a separate orientation term.
Style branches can be glabrous.
Corona lobes can be short. Comparisons such as 'shorter than anthers' are acceptable.
'Light coloured' means pale. Mapping it to high brightness is acceptable for a leaf, but a colour term would be better.
Leaflets can be trapezoid.
'Impressed' describes a ridge or groove on the pyrene surface, not the pyrene as a whole. A rule would need to attach it to the surface or ridge.
Leaf scars can be subcircular.
A fruit pedicel can be short.
The generic shape attribute fits compound shapes such as deltoid-elliptic on leaf scars.
Leaf scars can be triangular or deltoid.
A leaf (apex or margin) can be tri-toothed or tricuspidate. The examples are acceptable.
Cymes can be hairy. The examples are indumentum types, so the attribute is acceptable.
'Nodes 2-7 cm apart' gives the internode length, not a property of the node. Use internode length instead.
Stipules can be cup-shaped.
An epicalyx can have an entire margin or entire lobes. The examples are mostly about the margin.
The examples describe margins with spines, which looks like a leaf or other part, not a paraphysis. A rule would need to attach the quality to the margin and check the bearer.
Inflorescences can be brush-like.
A lamina can be dissected.
Valves can be twisted.
Fronds can be triangular or deltoid in outline.
A locule has a width. Some examples are dimension pairs, but they are acceptable.
The examples say 'ellipsoid', which is a different shape from prolate. This is a wrong reading. Use the ellipsoid term.
Shoot systems can be ridged.
Corolla lobes can be lanceolate-triangular. This is a compound shape that exists in PATO.
A spathe can be short. Some examples refer to the neck, which is a sub-part.
Cauline leaves can be lanceolate.
The counts are of stamens, stigmas and lodicules inside the floret, not of florets. This is the wrong part.
Follicles can be tomentose.
Staminodes can be terete.
A capsule can be narrow. Some examples refer to the neck, urn or teeth, which are sub-parts.
A flower bract can be short or shorter than the sepals.
Disc glands can have a 2-D shape such as rotund or ovate.
A spathe can be pubescent.
A spadix appendix can be long.
A grass leaf collar can be scabrid or smooth. The texture attribute fits.
A palea can be minutely bumpy. Knobbled is a loose match.
Trichomes are not papery. The example probably describes a bract or scale, so this is the wrong part.
An orchid labellum can be spatulate.
Leaflets can vary. The variant term is generic but acceptable.
What is inrolled is the spathe margin, not the spathe. A rule would need to attach the quality to the margin.
Nectaries, such as nectar scales, can be counted.
Peristome teeth can be bifid.
Stem nodes can be geniculate (bent).
A leaf apex, including its acumen or apiculus, can be short.
Fronds can be linear.
Vascular bundles or veins can radiate from the petiole. The reading is acceptable.
Ligules can be persistent or not.
Spikelets can be pedunculate.
Internodes can be spiny or prickly.
A hypanthium can be prickly.
A calyx can be translucent.
The annular part is the floral disk, not the whole flower. This is the wrong part. The pair belongs on the disk.
'Base spurred' says the base bears a spur. It does not say the base is spur-shaped, so this is a wrong reading.
